newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Independent Belgrade radio appeals to big powers.
newsitem.headline: Independent Belgrade radio appeals to big powers.

text.p: An independent Belgrade radio station shut down by Serbian authorities appealed to major powers on Wednesday to support free press and democractic reform in the Balkans.
Radio B-92 was knocked off the air on Tuesday by authorities determined to halt reporting on a wave of daily street demonstrations against President Slobodan Milosevic.
The radio staff issued a statement calling on countries attending this week's London conference on the Bosnia peace process to push for the station's "right to broadcast".
"The case of B-92 is not an isolated one," the statement said.
Another independent station in neighbouring Croatia has also come under severe pressure and a radio station in the Serbian town of Pozarevac was closed on Tuesday, the statement said.
Lasting peace in Bosnia could only be achieved if the world upheld democractic reform in the two most powerful countries in the region, Croatia and Bosnia.

"The stability which is needed to implement a reconstructuion programme in Bosnia successfully can only be reached if all human rights are respected and the cause of democracy is served," the radio said.
Saying it had strongly opposed Milosevic's "war-mongering policy", Radio B-92 said: "The truth was a victim of war and apparently is also a victim of peace".
Radio staff said they had been flooded with messages of support from abroad by fax, telephone and e-mail.
At the end of an opposition demonstration on Wednesday, supporters stood below the windows of opposition headquarters in Belgrade to listen to B-92 news over loudspeakers.
Federal ministry of communications authorities said in a statement they had no idea why Radio B-92 had stopped broadcasting.
The statement said the federal radio communications administration "does not know the reasons why radio B-92 had ceased transmitting" and that "the matter is not within our competence."
The radio's transmitter was switched off on Tuesday and federal authorities sent a letter saying B-92 was operating illegally.
A student radio station, which has legal permission to operate, was also effectively knocked off the air on Tuesday. Radio Index later resumed broadcasting but with an extremely weak signal.
From its cramped offices in the city centre, Radio B-92 has struggled to provide an alternative source of information to state television and radio since it was founded in 1989.
It lost much of its modest international funding this year when European countries chose to focus on media projects in Bosnia, radio staff said.
The radio, with a staff of about 75, was primarily relying on book publishing to pay for its news and music programmes.
The U.S. government's Voice of America said on Wednesday it would start broadcasting reports from B-92 radio's correspondents on medium and short-wave.
The broadcasts in Serbo-Croat would be easily accessible on car radios and the standard broadcast band, VOA officials said in Washington.
Veran Matic, editor-in-chief, said the radio station also had offers from Radio Free Europe and Deutsche Welle to rebroadcast B-92's news programme.
"In any case, we shall attempt to do our job and in practice wage a battle for freedom of speech which is especially threatened in Belgrade today."
